case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services v. Z.C.
key_cases.holding: In a class action on behalf of foster children whose Social Security benefits OCS applied to reimburse itself, the court held the due-process claim was not federally preempted and that OCS must give the notice ordered by the superior court if it continues its self-reimbursing representative-payee practice.
key_cases.relevance: A structural agency practice was exposed only by aggregating data across many children's cases.
key_cases.quote: We therefore hold that OCS must provide the notice ordered by the superior court if it wishes to continue implementing its self-reimbursing rep payee scheme.

key_cases.case_name: Basey v. State, Department of Public Safety, Division of Alaska State Troopers
key_cases.holding: The State failed to establish either the AS 40.25.122 litigation exception or the law-enforcement exception to the Alaska Public Records Act, so dismissal of the records requester's suit was error and the case was remanded.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the legal basis on which state child-welfare data and records can be compelled into public view.
key_cases.quote: We conclude it was error for the superior court to grant the State's motion to dismiss pursuant to AS 40.25.122.

key_cases.case_name: State v. Native Village of Tanana
key_cases.holding: Federally recognized Alaska Native tribes may exercise inherent sovereign jurisdiction to initiate ICWA child custody proceedings without a § 1918 reassumption petition, and judgments from those proceedings may be entitled to full faith and credit by the State.
key_cases.relevance: Shows that an Alaska decision chain is incomplete unless it models concurrent tribal jurisdiction alongside the state pathway.
key_cases.quote: federally recognized Alaska Native tribes are not necessarily precluded from exercising inherent sovereign jurisdiction to initiate "child custody proceedings" as ICWA defines that term

key_cases.holding: Alaska Native tribes possess inherent, non-territorial sovereign authority to adjudicate child custody disputes between their own members in tribal court, so the superior court erred in refusing to give the Northway Tribal Court judgment effect; the case was remanded to decide whether that judgment should be recognized under comity.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that an accurate Alaska decision chain must model a tribal-court pathway existing independently of reservation land and of any ICWA section 1918 reassumption petition.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that Native tribes do possess the inherent sovereign power to adjudicate child custody disputes between tribal members in their own courts

key_cases.case_name: State, Department of Health & Social Services, Division of Family & Youth Services v. Native Village of Curyung
key_cases.holding: Alaska Native villages may sue the Division's director in his official capacity under section 1983 as parens patriae on behalf of their member children to enforce rights created by the Adoption Assistance Act and ICWA — including the right to a case plan — but may not use section 1983 to enforce rights they hold as sovereigns and may not sue the State directly.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that systemic patterns across many children's cases are legally cognizable in Alaska when aggregated by a tribal plaintiff.
key_cases.quote: the villages may bring suit as parens patriae under § 1983 to enforce rights that are created by the Adoption Assistance Act and the Indian Child Welfare Act
